packet.headline_seed: China lands reusable rocket for first time, state media says
packet.description_seed: It follows similar landings of reusable rockets by US-owned companies SpaceX and Blue Origin.

what: China lands reusable rocket for first time, state media says

clean_source_blocks.text: It follows similar landings of reusable rockets by US-owned companies SpaceX and Blue Origin.

China has successfully landed a reusable rocket for the first time in a major breakthrough for the country's space programme, according to state media. The China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation said the Long March 10B rocket lifted off from Hainan in southern China at 12:15 local time (04:15GMT) on Friday. Around six minutes after separating from the rocket's upper stage, its booster returned to Earth vertically and was recovered on a floating platform. It signals that China may be able to challenge America's dominance in reusable rockets after successful landings by Elon Musk's SpaceX and Blue Origin, which is owned by Amazon founder Jeff Bezos. Rockets are typically considered expendable - their various segments being discarded and destroyed during ascent - which makes launching spacecraft expensive.

By reusing boosters - which are generally seen as the most valuable part of a rocket - the cost of satellite launches and space exploration can be significantly lowered. In December 2015, SpaceX landed a reusable Falcon 9 rocket from an orbital flight for the first time, followed by Blue Origin's New Glenn in November 2025. The Falcon 9 now launches about 150 times a year with boosters that are capable of being reused dozens of times. China made its first attempt at reusable rocket recovery in February, with a Long March 10A rocket. It completed a controlled descent and splashed down next to a recovery platform. The Long March 10B, which can carry a payload of at least 16 metric tons to low-Earth orbit, has been compared to SpaceX's Falcon 9.

The rocket meets the needs of various missions such as low Earth orbit satellite internet constellation deployment and large commercial satellite launches while also reducing costs, according to CASC, China’s state-owned main space contractor. CASC stated that it intended to reuse the first stage from today’s flight before the end of the year. https://t.co/jtCmasw3Y0 pic.twitter.com/ZsbVRk6FS0 “Going forward, the Long March 10B carrier rocket development team will continue to optimize rocket performance and accelerate the iterative upgrade of reusable rocket technology,” CASC stated. The recovery vessel is equipped with a flexible net capture system with hydraulic damping. The system means the first stage does not need landing legs, such as those used by the SpaceX Falcon 9 and Blue Origin’s New Glenn. China’s Long March ---

original_article.research:
[Lähde: BBC World]
China has successfully landed a reusable rocket for the first time in a major breakthrough for the country's space programme, according to state media.

The China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation said the Long March 10B rocket lifted off from Hainan in southern China at 12:15 local time (04:15GMT) on Friday.

Around six minutes after separating from the rocket's upper stage, its booster returned to Earth vertically and was recovered on a floating platform.

It signals that China may be able to challenge America's dominance in reusable rockets after successful landings by Elon Musk's SpaceX and Blue Origin, which is owned by Amazon founder Jeff Bezos.

Rockets are typically considered expendable - their various segments being discarded and destroyed during ascent - which makes launching spacecraft expensive.

By reusing boosters - which are generally seen as the most valuable part of a rocket - the cost of satellite launches and space exploration can be significantly lowered.

In December 2015, SpaceX landed a reusable Falcon 9 rocket from an orbital flight for the first time, followed by Blue Origin's New Glenn in November 2025.

The Falcon 9 now launches about 150 times a year with boosters that are capable of being reused dozens of times.

China made its first attempt at reusable rocket recovery in February, with a Long March 10A rocket. It completed a controlled descent and splashed down next to a recovery platform.

The Long March 10B, which can carry a payload of at least 16 metric tons to low-Earth orbit, has been compared to SpaceX's Falcon 9.

But unlike the Falcon 9, the Long March 10B does not autonomously land on a ground pad or drone ship. Instead "landing hooks" on the rocket catch a net attached to a floating platform.

Shares in Chinese space firms jumped following the news, with China Spacesat and China Satellite Communications each rising by 10%, the daily limit allowed by the country's financial market regulations.

---

[Lähde: SpaceNews]
HELSINKI — China launched its Long March 10B rocket early Friday and successfully recovered the first stage, marking a huge step for the country’s reusable rocket efforts.

The first Long March 10B rocket lifted off at 12:15 a.m. Eastern (0415 UTC) July 10 from Hainan Commercial Space Launch Site on the southern island province of Hainan. The China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation (CASC) confirmed the successful recovery of the rocket’s first stage 11 minutes later, using a sea platform equipped with a net capture system.

Videos emerging in the minutes following showed a controlled, powered descent with black smoke billowing from the top of the first stage, followed by capture by the Linghang Zhe (“navigator”) sea recovery vessel, with hooks deployed from the booster caught by a tensioned net. The recovery occurred six minutes after separation of the first and second stages.

The successful recovery sees CASC join U.S. companies SpaceX and Blue Origin in achieving recovery of an orbital booster.

The full success of the flight with insertion of an unnamed satellite into orbit was confirmed by CASC more than 90 minutes after liftoff, representing a huge boost to both China’s desire to develop reusable rocket capabilities, and for its crewed lunar program. CASC claimed the booster recovery to be the world’s first successful net-system recovery of a carrier rocket. The name, purpose and orbital parameters of the satellite were not disclosed.

The five-meter-diameter, two-stage Long March 10B is 63 meters long, with a mass of 760,000 kilograms at liftoff and has a low Earth orbit payload capacity of 16,000 kg in reusable mode.

The rocket meets the needs of various missions such as low Earth orbit satellite internet constellation deployment and large commercial satellite launches while also reducing costs, according to CASC, China’s state-owned main space contractor. CASC stated that it intended to reuse the first stage from today’s flight before the end of the year.

https://t.co/jtCmasw3Y0 pic.twitter.com/ZsbVRk6FS0

“Going forward, the Long March 10B carrier rocket development team will continue to optimize rocket performance and accelerate the iterative upgrade of reusable rocket technology,” CASC stated.

The recovery vessel is equipped with a flexible net capture system with hydraulic damping. The system means the first stage does not need landing legs, such as those used by the SpaceX Falcon 9 and Blue Origin’s New Glenn. China’s Long March

---

[Lähde: Scientific American]
China launches rival rocket to SpaceX Falcon 9 for the first time

China apparently didn’t issue any airspace or maritime notices ahead of the maiden launch of this rocket on Monday

By Claire Cameron edited by Jeanna Bryner

On Monday China launched its latest rocket, Long March 12B, for the first time with reportedly no advance warning. Typically, government space agencies and private space companies provide airspace and maritime warnings before launch—but state-owned rocket maker China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation (CASC) apparently did neither.

Airspace and maritime warnings are standard global safety procedures prior to rocket launches. The International Civil Aviation Organization and the International Maritime Organization normally issue such advance alerts to ensure air traffic and shipping can avoid potential hazards, such as falling debris, from a space launch. International law mandates that nation states are responsible for any damage that might be caused from rocket launches from their territory. Space analysts have previously warned that China doesn’t always fully abide by these international norms, however, especially when it comes to safely disposing of debris from its rocket launches.

The spacecraft, which is similar in capability to SpaceX’s Falcon 9, lifted off at 4:40 A.M. EDT from the Dongfeng Commercial Aerospace Innovation Test Zone in the Gobi Desert, with news of the launch spreading first on Chinese social media, according to SpaceNews.

payload.title: Kiina palautti uudelleenkäytettävän rakettivaiheen ensi kertaa
payload.summary: Long March 10B -raketin ensimmäinen vaihe laskeutui pystysuoraan merellä olevalle alustalle. CASC aikoo käyttää talteen otettua vaihetta uudelleen jo ennen vuoden loppua.
payload.content:
Kiina on onnistunut ensimmäistä kertaa palauttamaan uudelleenkäytettävän rakettivaiheen laskeutumisalustalle, maan valtionmedia kertoi. Long March 10B -raketin ensimmäinen vaihe palasi pystysuoraan merellä olevalle alustalle noin kuusi minuuttia sen jälkeen, kun se oli irronnut raketin ylemmästä vaiheesta. Onnistuminen on merkittävä askel Kiinan avaruusohjelmalle.

## Rakettivaihe otettiin talteen merellä

Kiinan valtiollisen avaruusalan pääurakoitsijan CASC:n mukaan Long March 10B laukaistiin perjantaina kello 12.15 paikallista aikaa Hainanista Etelä-Kiinasta. Palautunut ensimmäinen vaihe laskeutui kelluvalle alukselle, jonka joustava verkkojärjestelmä ja hydraulinen vaimennus ottivat sen vastaan. Järjestelmän ansiosta rakettivaiheessa ei tarvita SpaceX:n Falcon 9:n ja Blue Originin New Glennin käyttämiä laskeutumisjalkoja.

CASC ilmoitti aikovansa käyttää lennolta palautettua ensimmäistä vaihetta uudelleen ennen vuoden loppua. Yhtiön mukaan Long March 10B:n suorituskykyä kehitetään edelleen ja uudelleenkäytettävän rakettitekniikan päivityksiä nopeutetaan. Raketti pystyy kuljettamaan vähintään 16 tonnin hyötykuorman matalalle Maan kiertoradalle.

CASC:n mukaan raketti soveltuu esimerkiksi matalan kiertoradan satelliitti-internetverkostojen rakentamiseen sekä suurten kaupallisten satelliittien laukaisemiseen. Long March 10B:tä on verrattu yhdysvaltalaisen SpaceX:n Falcon 9 -rakettiin, joka on keskeinen osa yhtiön toistuvia satelliitti- ja avaruuslentoja.

## Uudelleenkäyttö voi pienentää kustannuksia

Kantorakettien osat ovat perinteisesti olleet kertakäyttöisiä: ne hylätään ja tuhoutuvat laukaisun aikana. Ensimmäistä vaihetta pidetään yleensä raketin arvokkaimpana osana, joten sen käyttäminen useita kertoja voi alentaa merkittävästi satelliittilaukaisujen ja avaruustutkimuksen kustannuksia. SpaceX palautti kiertoratalennolla käytetyn Falcon 9:n ensimmäisen vaiheen ensi kertaa joulukuussa 2015. Falcon 9 lentää nykyisin noin 150 kertaa vuodessa, ja sen vaiheita voidaan käyttää kymmeniä kertoja.

Blue Origin puolestaan onnistui New Glenn -rakettinsa palautuksessa marraskuussa 2025. Kiina teki oman ensimmäisen palautusyrityksensä helmikuussa Long March 10A -raketilla. Sen ensimmäinen vaihe suoritti hallitun laskeutumisen, mutta putosi mereen palautusalustan viereen. Long March 10B:n onnistunut talteenotto vie Kiinaa lähemmäksi yhdysvaltalaisyhtiöiden saavuttamaa uudelleenkäytettävien rakettien osaamista ja voi vahvistaa sen asemaa satelliittien kaupallisissa laukaisuissa.
summary_bullets: Long March 10B:n ensimmäinen vaihe laskeutui pystysuoraan kelluvalle palautusalustalle.
CASC aikoo käyttää talteen otettua rakettivaihetta uudelleen ennen vuoden loppua.
Uudelleenkäytettävä tekniikka voi alentaa satelliittien ja muiden hyötykuormien laukaisukustannuksia.
payload.journalist_note: Onnistuminen perustuu CASC:n ilmoitukseen ja Kiinan valtionmedian tietoihin. Tapahtumasta ei ole paketissa riippumatonta teknistä vahvistusta.

It follows similar landings of reusable rockets by US-owned companies SpaceX and Blue Origin.

China has successfully landed a reusable rocket for the first time in a major breakthrough for the country's space programme, according to state media. The China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation said the Long March 10B rocket lifted off from Hainan in southern China at 12:15 local time (04:15GMT) on Friday. Around six minutes after separating from the rocket's upper stage, its booster returned to Earth vertically and was recovered on a floating platform. It signals that China may be able to challenge America's dominance in reusable rockets after successful landings by Elon Musk's SpaceX and Blue Origin, which is owned by Amazon founder Jeff Bezos. Rockets are typically considered expendable - their various segments being discarded and destroyed during ascent - which makes launching spacecraft expensive.

By reusing boosters - which are generally seen as the most valuable part of a rocket - the cost of satellite launches and space exploration can be significantly lowered. In December 2015, SpaceX landed a reusable Falcon 9 rocket from an orbital flight for the first time, followed by Blue Origin's New Glenn in November 2025. The Falcon 9 now launches about 150 times a year with boosters that are capable of being reused dozens of times. China made its first attempt at reusable rocket recovery in February, with a Long March 10A rocket. It completed a controlled descent and splashed down next to a recovery platform. The Long March 10B, which can carry a payload of at least 16 metric tons to low-Earth orbit, has been compared to SpaceX's Falcon 9.

The rocket meets the needs of various missions such as low Earth orbit satellite internet constellation deployment and large commercial satellite launches while also reducing costs, according to CASC, China’s state-owned main space contractor. CASC stated that it intended to reuse the first stage from today’s flight before the end of the year. https://t.co/jtCmasw3Y0 pic.twitter.com/ZsbVRk6FS0 “Going forward, the Long March 10B carrier rocket development team will continue to optimize rocket performance and accelerate the iterative upgrade of reusable rocket technology,” CASC stated. The recovery vessel is equipped with a flexible net capture system with hydraulic damping.
